title: What the Train Cannot Copy
paragraphs: In 1912 the surgeon Alexis Carrel, a Nobel laureate that same year, began growing cells from a chick embryo heart in glass flasks.
The culture was fed and divided for 34 years, outliving Carrel himself, and it became the standard proof that cells freed from the body could divide forever.

Then, in 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead at the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia reported that normal human fetal cells divided roughly 50 times and then stopped, however carefully they were fed.
The cells did not die; they entered a state now called replicative senescence, alive and metabolically active but finished with division.

The ceiling came to be known as the Hayflick limit, and the chick heart was explained away: the embryo extract that fed the culture had most likely carried fresh cells into the flask with every feeding.
I find something admirable in a young scientist telling his field that its favorite experiment was wrong.
A decade later the limit acquired a possible mechanism, found by thinking about copying rather than aging.
DNA polymerase, the enzyme that duplicates a chromosome, can only add to the end of an existing strand, so it needs a short RNA primer to start, and it builds in one direction only.
On one strand this causes no trouble, but on the other the enzyme works backward in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, each begun by its own primer.
When the primer at the very tip is removed, there is no strand upstream to extend into the gap, and a short stretch at the end goes uncopied.
Every round of replication should therefore leave the chromosome slightly shorter.

The Russian biologist Alexey Olovnikov is said to have grasped this in 1971 while waiting for a Moscow subway train, picturing the polymerase as a train that cannot copy the track beneath it, and he proposed that the steady loss of the ends might be the counter behind Hayflick's limit.
Chromosome ends had been singled out as special a generation earlier.

In 1938 the geneticist Hermann Muller, who had been breaking fruit fly chromosomes with X-rays, noted that broken ends were sticky and tended to fuse with other broken ends, while the natural ends never did.
He coined the word telomere for the natural end, from the Greek for end and part.
Around the same time Barbara McClintock, working with maize, watched broken ends fuse and then tear apart at the next division, a cycle that natural ends were somehow spared.
Something at the tip was protecting it, but nobody knew what the tip was made of.
The answer came from a pond.

Tetrahymena thermophila is a single-celled ciliate that swims in fresh water and carries, in one of its two nuclei, many thousands of tiny linear chromosomes, so every cell holds an enormous number of chromosome ends.

In the late 1970s Elizabeth Blackburn, a postdoctoral researcher in Joseph Gall's laboratory at Yale, sequenced the ends of these molecules; her 1978 paper reported a simple sequence, TTGGGG, repeated over and over.
A decade later the human version turned up: the same kind of repeat, TTAGGG, copied hundreds to thousands of times at the end of every chromosome.
Jack Szostak, at Harvard Medical School, had found that linear DNA put into yeast cells was chewed up or stitched onto other chromosomes.
After hearing Blackburn speak at a 1980 meeting, he proposed capping his linear yeast DNA with the Tetrahymena repeats to see whether it survived.
It did.
Their 1982 paper showed that a ciliate's chromosome ends could protect DNA inside a yeast, the first sign that telomeres worked by a mechanism shared across kingdoms.
The experiment held a quieter clue: over time the yeast cells added their own repeats onto the borrowed Tetrahymena ends, which no known copying mechanism could explain.
An enzyme that built telomeres from scratch, Blackburn and Szostak reasoned, had to exist.
Finding it fell to Carol Greider, a graduate student who joined Blackburn's laboratory at Berkeley in 1984.
She mixed Tetrahymena extracts with a synthetic DNA ending in the telomere repeat, added nucleotides, and looked for anything that lengthened it.
On December 25, 1984, she developed an X-ray film and saw a ladder of bands climbing the gel in steps of six: the extract was adding TTGGGG repeats one after another.
They published the finding in 1985 and named the activity telomere terminal transferase, soon shortened to telomerase.

Two further results made the enzyme stranger and more elegant: its activity vanished when RNA was destroyed, so it was part protein and part RNA, and that RNA carried a stretch complementary to the repeat, a built-in template the enzyme reads to decide what to add.
The picture that emerged is of a reverse transcriptase, an enzyme that makes DNA by reading RNA, carrying its own instructions.
Telomerase has two essential components: a protein subunit, now called TERT, that performs the chemistry, and an RNA subunit, TERC, that supplies the template.
The RNA pairs with the chromosome's overhanging end, the protein extends that end by copying the template, the enzyme slides forward, and the cycle repeats.
The end-replication problem is not abolished by this arrangement; it is paid for in advance, with a buffer of disposable repeats that can be topped up when a cell has the enzyme to do it.

The two stories met in 1990, when Calvin Harley, Bruce Futcher, and Greider measured telomeres in cultured human fibroblasts and found that they shrank with every division, a loss now put at roughly 50 to 200 base pairs per division.
Most ordinary cells make little or no telomerase, so their ends run down with use; the cells that must divide indefinitely, including germ cells and some stem cells, keep the enzyme switched on.

In 1998 researchers reported that adding the TERT gene to normal human cells let them sail past the Hayflick limit with no sign of senescence, the strongest evidence yet that the shrinking ends were the counter Olovnikov had imagined.
Too little telomerase ends a cell's working life; too much has consequences of its own.

Roughly 85 to 90 percent of human cancers show telomerase activity, having switched the enzyme back on to become immortal; most of the rest maintain their ends by a recombination route called alternative lengthening of telomeres.

The opposite extreme is dyskeratosis congenita, a rare inherited disorder marked by abnormal skin pigmentation, misshapen nails, white patches in the mouth, and, most dangerously, failure of the bone marrow; its known causes are mutations in genes that build or maintain telomeres, including the components of telomerase, and patients' telomeres are abnormally short.
The enzyme is therefore both a target to inhibit, in tumors, and a deficiency to correct, in a few inherited diseases, and a treatment aimed at one must be watched for the other.
It is a short step from these facts to the claim that telomeres are the clock of human aging, a step taken constantly, often by people with something to sell.
I am wary of it.
Laboratory mice carry telomeres several times longer than ours and live about two years, and mice engineered to lack telomerase stayed largely healthy for several generations before defects appeared.
Telomere length also varies widely among healthy people of the same age, which makes it a poor ruler for any one individual.

Replicative senescence is real, and it very likely protects us from cancer by retiring overworked cells; whether it also drives the decline of a whole organism is a genuinely open question, not a settled one.
In 2009 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Blackburn, Greider, and Szostak for the discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase.

The prize had the shape of the work: a theorist on a subway platform saw the flaw, a pond ciliate supplied the sequence, a yeast showed the fix was ancient, and a graduate student working through a holiday caught the enzyme in the act.
What strikes me is how little of this was aimed at aging or cancer and how much of both it explained; the question that mattered was simply how a chromosome keeps its ends.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when the cells studied by Hayflick and Moorhead reached their limit, they
choices: died within a few days of their final division
fused with one another and tore apart at the next division
stayed alive and active but no longer divided
resumed dividing only when fresh embryo extract was added
transformed into cancer cells that switched telomerase on

proof.quote: alive and metabolically active but finished with division

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the cells did not die; they entered replicative senescence, alive and metabolically active but finished with division.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 1 says plainly that the cells did not die.
Wrong paragraph: fusing and tearing apart is McClintock's maize observation in paragraph 3.
Reversed: the cells stopped no matter how carefully they were fed, and embryo extract belongs to Carrel's story.
Outside the passage: nothing says the senescent cells became cancerous; telomerase in cancer is a separate point in paragraph 9.

questions.stem: The author describes Alexis Carrel's chick heart culture in paragraph 1 primarily to
choices: present the accepted belief that Hayflick's finding overturned
show that cells from birds divide more times than cells from humans
credit Carrel with the first measurement of the Hayflick limit
argue that Nobel Prize winners are rarely questioned by younger scientists
explain how embryo extract keeps cultured cells alive and dividing

proof.quote: it became the standard proof that cells freed from the body could divide forever
Then, in 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the chick heart became the standard proof that cells could divide forever, and the very next sentence opens with 'Then, in 1961' and Hayflick's contrary result. Carrel is there as the belief being overturned.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the chick culture is explained by fresh cells in the extract, not by any difference between birds and humans.
Wrong person: paragraph 1 credits Hayflick and Moorhead, and Carrel's result was the opposite of a limit.
Too strong: the author admires Hayflick for questioning his field but never generalizes about Nobel winners.
Half right: the extract matters, but as the suspected source of fresh cells, not as something the author sets out to explain.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if Carrel's culture had been fed an extract containing no living cells, the culture would most likely have
choices: continued dividing for 34 years just as it did
produced abnormally short telomeres within a few divisions
fused its chromosome ends into a destructive cycle
entered a state of senescence and kept dividing slowly
stopped dividing after a limited number of doublings

proof.quote: carried fresh cells into the flask with every feeding
divided roughly 50 times and then stopped

questions.why: Paragraph 1 explains the chick heart's apparent immortality by fresh cells arriving with every feeding of embryo extract. Take those away and the culture is just ordinary cells, which, as Hayflick found, divide a limited number of times and then stop.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the 34 years depended on the fresh cells the extract carried in.
Outside the passage: no telomere measurement is tied to Carrel's culture, and the shortening in paragraph 8 is gradual.
Wrong paragraph: fusion of broken ends is McClintock's observation in paragraph 3, not a result of changing a culture's food.
Half wrong: paragraph 1 says senescent cells are finished with division, not dividing slowly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a short stretch of DNA at the chromosome tip goes uncopied because
choices: the enzyme that removes RNA primers also digests the DNA beneath them
no strand lies upstream of the last primer's gap for the enzyme to extend
the polymerase adds nucleotides only to the beginning of a strand, never its end
the polymerase builds in both directions and its two copies collide at the tip
the RNA primer at the tip is never removed and blocks the final copy

proof.quote: there is no strand upstream to extend into the gap

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says that when the primer at the very tip is removed, there is no strand upstream to extend into the gap, so that stretch goes uncopied.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing says primer removal digests DNA; the problem is the gap left behind.
Reversed: paragraph 2 says the polymerase can only add to the end of an existing strand.
Reversed: paragraph 2 says the polymerase can build in only one direction.
Reversed: the trouble begins precisely when the final primer is removed.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 2, the word 'counter' most nearly means
choices: a flat surface across which goods are sold
a reply made in order to oppose an argument
a small disc used as a token in a game
a mechanism that keeps a running tally
a cook's work surface in a kitchen

proof.quote: the steady loss of the ends might be the counter behind Hayflick's limit

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the steady loss of the ends might be the counter behind Hayflick's limit: each division removes a little more, so the shrinking ends keep count of how many divisions have happened. The shop or kitchen surface is the everyday meaning and makes no sense here.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning, but nothing in the sentence is being sold or served.
The word can mean a rebuttal, but Olovnikov is proposing a mechanism for the limit, not arguing against it.
A game token is another meaning, but the sentence describes a process that tallies divisions, not a piece.
Another everyday meaning that has no place in a sentence about chromosome ends.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Hermann Muller observed that
choices: broken ends fused with other broken ends, while natural ends did not
natural ends of chromosomes turned sticky after exposure to X-rays
broken ends in maize fused and then tore apart at the following division
the natural ends of fruit fly chromosomes carried a short repeated sequence
chromosomes that lost their natural ends could no longer be copied

proof.quote: broken ends were sticky and tended to fuse with other broken ends, while the natural ends never did

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Muller, breaking fruit fly chromosomes with X-rays, noted that broken ends were sticky and tended to fuse with other broken ends, while the natural ends never did.
distractorNotes: Reversed: it was the broken ends that were sticky, and the natural ends never fused.
Wrong person: the fuse-and-tear cycle in maize is McClintock's observation.
Wrong era: the repeated sequence was not found until Blackburn's work in paragraph 4, and Muller did not know what the tip was made of.
Outside the passage: the copying problem belongs to paragraph 2 and was not Muller's observation.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about Tetrahymena thermophila EXCEPT:
choices: It is a single-celled organism that lives in fresh water.
Each of its cells holds an enormous number of chromosome ends.
Its chromosome ends consist of the sequence TTGGGG repeated over and over.
It added its own repeats onto the ends of borrowed yeast DNA.
Its chromosome ends protected linear DNA that was placed inside yeast cells.

proof.quote: single-celled ciliate that swims in fresh water
every cell holds an enormous number of chromosome ends
TTGGGG, repeated over and over
a ciliate's chromosome ends could protect DNA inside a yeast
the yeast cells added their own repeats onto the borrowed Tetrahymena ends

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says it was the yeast cells that added their own repeats onto the borrowed Tetrahymena ends, not the other way around. The other four statements come straight from paragraphs 4 and 5.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4, sentence 2 calls it a single-celled ciliate that swims in fresh water.
Paragraph 4, sentence 2 says every cell holds an enormous number of chromosome ends.
Paragraph 4, sentence 3 reports the sequence TTGGGG repeated over and over.
Paragraph 5, sentence 4 says a ciliate's chromosome ends could protect DNA inside a yeast.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what Carol Greider saw on December 25, 1984, was
choices: a synthetic DNA strand that had been digested into fragments of six
a ladder of bands climbing up the gel in steps of six
an RNA molecule containing a stretch complementary to the repeat
yeast colonies whose chromosomes carried Tetrahymena repeats
a protein subunit that lengthened DNA without any template

proof.quote: saw a ladder of bands climbing the gel in steps of six

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says that on December 25, 1984, Greider developed an X-ray film and saw a ladder of bands climbing the gel in steps of six, the sign that something was adding TTGGGG repeats one after another.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the DNA was being lengthened, not digested.
Wrong timing: the RNA template was one of the two further results described later in paragraph 6.
Wrong paragraph: the yeast experiment belongs to Szostak in paragraph 5.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 says the enzyme is part RNA and reads a built-in template.

questions.stem: Suppose a researcher alters the RNA subunit of telomerase in a yeast cell so that part of its template region carries a different sequence. Based on the passage, the repeats newly added to that cell's chromosome ends would most likely
choices: be unchanged, because the protein subunit decides what sequence is added
stop being added, because the protein subunit can only read DNA
switch to the Tetrahymena sequence TTGGGG regardless of the change
shrink by about 50 to 200 base pairs with each cell division
match the new sequence written into the altered template

proof.quote: a built-in template the enzyme reads to decide what to add
an RNA subunit, TERC, that supplies the template

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the RNA carries a built-in template that the enzyme reads to decide what to add, and paragraph 7 says the RNA subunit supplies the template. Change the template and the enzyme copies the new sequence into the chromosome ends.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 7 gives the protein the chemistry and the RNA the template.
Contradicted: paragraph 7 calls telomerase a reverse transcriptase, an enzyme that makes DNA by reading RNA.
Wrong organism: TTGGGG is the Tetrahymena repeat, and the enzyme copies whatever template it carries.
Wrong paragraph: shrinking is what happens to human fibroblasts without telomerase in paragraph 8.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1990 study by Harley, Futcher, and Greider found that
choices: human fibroblasts with added TERT divided past the Hayflick limit
germ cells and stem cells keep telomerase switched on throughout life
telomeres in cultured human fibroblasts shrank with every division
roughly 85 to 90 percent of human tumors contain active telomerase
Tetrahymena extracts added TTGGGG repeats to synthetic DNA

proof.quote: measured telomeres in cultured human fibroblasts and found that they shrank with every division

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says that in 1990 Harley, Futcher, and Greider measured telomeres in cultured human fibroblasts and found that they shrank with every division.
distractorNotes: Wrong year: the TERT experiment is the 1998 result later in paragraph 8.
Stated in paragraph 8, but as general background, not as the 1990 study's finding.
Wrong paragraph: the cancer figure is in paragraph 9 and is not credited to this study.
Wrong study: that is Greider's 1984 observation in paragraph 6.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a line of germ cells, compared with a line of ordinary skin cells, would most likely
choices: maintain the length of its chromosome ends across many divisions
lose about 50 to 200 base pairs from each chromosome end per division
reach the Hayflick limit after roughly 50 divisions
require an added TERT gene in order to keep dividing
rely on recombination to maintain its chromosome ends

proof.quote: the cells that must divide indefinitely, including germ cells and some stem cells, keep the enzyme switched on
a buffer of disposable repeats that can be topped up when a cell has the enzyme to do it

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says most ordinary cells make little or no telomerase, so their ends run down, while germ cells keep the enzyme switched on. Paragraph 7 says the enzyme tops up the disposable repeats, so germ cells should hold their ends steady where skin cells lose ground.
distractorNotes: Reversed: that steady loss is what paragraph 8 describes for cells without telomerase.
Reversed: the limit belongs to the ordinary cells whose ends run down.
Reversed: germ cells already have telomerase switched on, so nothing needs to be added.
Wrong paragraph: recombination is the route some cancers use in paragraph 9, not germ cells.

questions.stem: According to the passage, approximately what share of human cancers show telomerase activity?
choices: fewer than 10 percent
about one third
roughly half
somewhere between 50 and 60 percent
roughly 85 to 90 percent

proof.quote: Roughly 85 to 90 percent of human cancers show telomerase activity

questions.why: Paragraph 9 gives the figure directly: roughly 85 to 90 percent of human cancers show telomerase activity, and most of the rest use a recombination-based route.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the minority without telomerase, not the majority, is about this small.
Not in the passage: no one-third figure appears anywhere.
Too low: paragraph 9 says the large majority, not half.
Not in the passage: the only cancer figure given is 85 to 90 percent.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of dyskeratosis congenita EXCEPT:
choices: It is marked by white patches in the mouth.
Patients' telomeres are unusually long.
Its most dangerous feature is failure of the bone marrow.
It is a rare inherited disorder.
Its causes include mutations in telomerase components.

proof.quote: white patches in the mouth
most dangerously, failure of the bone marrow
a rare inherited disorder
including the components of telomerase
patients' telomeres are abnormally short

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says patients' telomeres are abnormally short, the opposite of long. The other four statements all appear in that same sentence.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 9, sentence 3 lists white patches in the mouth among its marks.
Paragraph 9, sentence 3 names bone marrow failure as the most dangerous feature.
Paragraph 9, sentence 3 calls it a rare inherited disorder.
Paragraph 9, sentence 3 traces its known causes to genes including the components of telomerase.

questions.stem: The author mentions laboratory mice in paragraph 10 primarily to
choices: show that telomerase is unnecessary for the health of mammals
explain why mice are the preferred animal for telomere research
propose that mice age more slowly than their telomeres would predict
cast doubt on the claim that telomere length sets the pace of aging
argue that human telomeres should be lengthened to match those of mice

proof.quote: the claim that telomeres are the clock of human aging
Laboratory mice carry telomeres several times longer than ours and live about two years

questions.why: Paragraph 10 opens with the claim that telomeres are the clock of aging, the author says 'I am wary of it,' and the mice come next: long telomeres, short lives, and health without telomerase for generations. They are evidence against the clock claim.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the mice stayed largely healthy for several generations before defects appeared, so the enzyme is not unnecessary.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about which animal researchers prefer.
Reversed: the mice live about two years despite long telomeres, which is faster, not slower, than a telomere clock would predict.
Outside the passage: the author never recommends lengthening human telomeres and is wary of such claims.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that mice engineered to lack telomerase remained largely healthy for several generations most likely because
choices: mice rely on recombination rather than telomerase to maintain their ends
mouse cells do not shorten their chromosome ends when they divide
their unusually long telomeres took several generations to run down
defects in mice appear only after the Hayflick limit of 50 divisions
replicative senescence does not occur in animals that live two years

proof.quote: Laboratory mice carry telomeres several times longer than ours
a buffer of disposable repeats
make little or no telomerase, so their ends run down with use

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says mouse telomeres are several times longer than ours, and paragraphs 7 and 8 describe telomeres as a buffer that runs down when a cell lacks the enzyme. A much bigger buffer takes much longer to spend, which is why the defects took generations to show.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: recombination is the route some cancers use in paragraph 9; nothing attributes it to mice.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 says every round of replication shortens the chromosome, and the defects did eventually appear.
Mash-up: the Hayflick limit counts divisions of cultured human cells, not generations of mice.
Too strong and unsupported: the passage never says senescence is absent in short-lived animals.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that telomeres are the clock of human aging is best described as
choices: approving
skeptical
detached
nostalgic
alarmed

proof.quote: often by people with something to sell
I am wary of it.
a genuinely open question, not a settled one

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the step to the aging-clock claim is taken constantly, often by people with something to sell, then states 'I am wary of it' and closes by calling the question open, not settled. That is a skeptic's voice: doubting without dismissing.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author resists the claim rather than endorsing it.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position in the first person.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 10 looks back fondly on anything.
Too strong: the author is measured and calls the question open, not dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Carol Greider's Christmas Day discovery of telomerase was the most important single event in the history of molecular biology
The end-replication problem proves that telomere shortening is the clock that drives human aging and that switching on telomerase would reverse it
Alexis Carrel's chick heart culture misled biologists for decades until Hayflick's experiment showed that cells can divide only a limited number of times
A long inquiry into how chromosomes keep their ends explained both the division limit and cancer's immortality, while its link to aging stays open
Tetrahymena thermophila was chosen for telomere research because its cells carry more chromosome ends than those of any other organism on Earth

proof.quote: The ceiling came to be known as the Hayflick limit
the strongest evidence yet that the shrinking ends were the counter Olovnikov had imagined
a genuinely open question, not a settled one
the question that mattered was simply how a chromosome keeps its ends

questions.why: The passage follows one question, how a chromosome keeps its ends, from Hayflick's limit through telomerase to cancer, and paragraphs 10 and 11 close by separating what the work explained from the aging claim the author calls open.
distractorNotes: Too strong and never said: the author admires Greider's experiment but ranks nothing as the most important event in the field.
Reversed: paragraph 10 says the author is wary of the aging-clock claim and calls it an open question.
Too narrow: Carrel and Hayflick fill only the first of eleven paragraphs.
Too narrow and too strong: the passage says Tetrahymena holds an enormous number of ends, not more than any other organism, and that is one detail among many.
